claims.text: An uncertainty-aware, ML-enhanced atomistic framework integrating DFT, MD, and quantum simulation can predict the electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr within ±5% of experiment.
The ±5% accuracy applies to both nominally pure HfNbTaTiZr and material containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The ±5% accuracy applies over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The framework will explicitly model substitutional and interstitial oxygen defects and their associated local lattice distortions.
Quantum effects in the 0–200 K regime include localized vibrational or tunneling states.
Anharmonic lattice vibrations, phonon-impurity scattering, and defect diffusion are relevant in the 300–1200 K regime.
Oxygen impurities induce local atomic-scale distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen-induced distortions create non-uniform vibrational modes that act as scattering centers affecting electrical conductivity.
At low temperatures, path-integral MD or similar quantum methods can accurately capture defect-induced quantum vibrational states.
Defect-induced quantum vibrational states alter electron or phonon transport.
At high temperatures, the framework can capture strong anharmonic phonon scattering and thermal expansion effects enhanced by oxygen defects.
Accounting for these quantum, anharmonic, and defect effects will improve accuracy relative to defect-free analytical models.
The framework will reproduce the distinctive temperature-dependent conductivity behavior observed in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
If the held-out 300 K conductivity is 150 S/cm, a prediction outside 135–165 S/cm constitutes a deviation greater than ±10%.
Existing analytical models assume perfect, defect-free crystals and omit localized defect-induced effects.
Omission of localized defect effects causes significant deviations in analytical predictions of electrical conductivity.
The framework is applicable only to bulk HfNbTaTiZr at 0–200 K or 300–1200 K and oxygen levels no greater than 1 wt.%.
Temperatures or oxygen levels outside the stated boundaries may introduce complexities that compromise prediction accuracy.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis requires predictions within ±5%, but the numerical falsification rule rejects only deviations greater than ±10%. A 6–10% error would violate the stated hypothesis without meeting the stated numerical falsification criterion.
